items.name: kernel-borderlands
items.description: Kernel-level runtime defense framework that detects, classifies and contains anomalous process behaviour at Ring 0 on Linux.
items.body:
## What it is

Kernel Borderlands (KB) is a runtime defense framework that watches a Linux system from inside the kernel. It detects, classifies and contains anomalous process behaviour at **Ring 0**.

Instead of leaning only on signatures or fixed rules, KB observes kernel telemetry through **eBPF instrumentation**, builds behavioural context from it, and uses that to decide how to respond while the system is running. It is built for research and experimentation into host defense.

## How it is put together

- **Sensors** (C, eBPF with CO-RE and libbpf) observe the kernel and collect telemetry.
- **Control plane** (Go): the `kbd` daemon scores what the sensors report and enforces the response.
- **Operator tools:** the `kbctl` command line, a web dashboard and an SSH console.
- **Containment is deliberate.** Isolate is reversible, namespace-level containment. Kill is separate, needs a two-click confirmation, and only goes ahead after `kbd` has passed its own safety checks and the sensor has confirmed it applied the containment. PID 1, kernel threads, protected executables and registered workloads are never killed.
- **Research components** sit alongside: a Python agent swarm for behavioural reasoning and multi-agent reinforcement learning, and a Rust script checker. Both are installed but kept off by default for now.

## Installing it

Version 1.0.0 is the first release, packaged for Ubuntu 24.04 and Debian (`.deb`) and for Arch (`.pkg.tar.zst`), with checksums to verify the download and a field manual for each distribution covering installation, operation and the command reference. Nothing starts at install time: run `sudo kbctl up`, then `kbctl dashboard open`.

It needs a Linux kernel with BTF, `bpf` enabled in the LSM list (the docs explain how), systemd and openssh. The `docs/` folder in the repository covers the architecture, hook points and development setup.
items.install:
# Ubuntu 24.04 / Debian
sudo apt install ./kernel-borderlands_1.0.0_amd64.deb

# Arch
sudo pacman -U kernel-borderlands-1.0.0-1-x86_64.pkg.tar.zst

# nothing starts on install
sudo kbctl up
kbctl dashboard open

items.name: kblinuxv-archives
items.description: Archive of Linux vulnerability reproduction artifacts preserved for research, analysis and reproducibility.
items.body:
## What it is

KB-LVA is the Kernel Borderlands Linux Vulnerability Archive: an independent research dataset of Linux vulnerability proof-of-concepts and reproduction artifacts, kept with enough provenance and verification evidence for other researchers to study and reproduce them.

Finding a CVE does not mean finding a usable reproduction artifact. KB-LVA records where each artifact came from, what it is, whether it matches the CVE, whether it is still available, and whether anyone has reproduced it. The main deliverable is a machine-readable dataset: PoC source files where redistribution is permitted, plus vulnerability records, provenance, compatibility, integrity hashes, license status and verification evidence.

## How it works

Each artifact moves through discovery, classification, deduplication, a human decision to acquire, retrieval from the original repository at an immutable commit, integrity and provenance checks, source review, validation in an isolated lab, and finally a versioned release. Its state is one of `DISCOVERED`, `RETRIEVED`, `SOURCE_REVIEWED`, `LAB_VALIDATED` or `REJECTED`. Acquiring something is not validating it.

The pipeline is a single Go command-line tool, `kblva`. Automation prepares changes on separate branches and opens pull requests, but a person decides, and automation never runs a PoC.

## Limits and safety

KB-LVA is not a scanner, an exploit framework or a place to run proof-of-concepts. Collected artifacts keep their original licenses and attribution. Where a license is unknown or restrictive, only metadata and a source reference are kept. Nothing from the archive should be run outside an isolated lab.
items.install:
make build
bin/kblva doctor
bin/kblva run

items.name: emrac
items.description: Hybrid package-management platform for Arch Linux covering discovery, build, install and maintenance across repositories and the AUR.
items.body:
## What it is

Emrac is a hybrid package manager for Arch Linux. It is an orchestration and interface layer over `pacman`, `makepkg`, `libalpm`, PKGBUILD and the AUR, and it puts the official repositories, the AUR and local repositories behind one command line.

It builds from a PKGBUILD when that is worthwhile, installs a binary when it is not, and tells you why. Every change shows a plan first, and `--dry-run` works on all of them.

## Installing it

On Arch Linux, or an Arch-based system, the install script downloads the release tarball, checks its SHA-256 against the value pinned inside the script, builds a pacman package from it, and installs that with `sudo pacman -U`. Because pacman tracks every file, `sudo pacman -Rns emrac` removes it cleanly. The script never runs as root, asks for `sudo` only where pacman needs it, and cleans up after itself.

It is meant to be read before it is run, so the quick start downloads it and opens it first. `sh install.sh --dry-run` shows what it would do, and `sh install.sh --uninstall` removes the package. The AUR package is not published yet.

## Checking your system with doctor

`emrac doctor` runs read-only health checks and suggests a fix for each finding. It looks at dependencies and databases, pending upgrades against freshly synced repositories, the running kernel, disk space, caches, orphaned packages, `.pacnew` files, failed units, pins and the build sandbox. It can also write a sanitized bug report. It changes nothing, so it is a safe first command on a new machine.

## What it adds

- **Plans that match pacman.** Upgrade previews are built from repositories synced just now, including what conflicts and replacements will remove, so what you confirm is what happens.
- **AUR builds you can trust a little more.** Packages are reviewed, audited for risky code, built in a bubblewrap sandbox, and inspected again before they are installed.
- **A history you can check.** Each record is linked to the one before by SHA-256, and a second copy is kept in a root-owned ledger, so edits and deletions show up.
- **Undo.** Transactions can be rolled back or redone, and the installed set can be saved and restored.
- **Everyday tools:** `.pacnew` handling, cache management, pins, and Arch news that can stop an upgrade.

The current release is slice r3 (version 0.3.0, 2026-10-15). The core loop works, and a terminal interface and build profiles are still to come.
items.install:
# install on Arch Linux: read the script first, then run it
curl -fsSLO https://pardhuvarmax.github.io/emrac/install.sh
less install.sh
sh install.sh            # asks before it does anything (--dry-run shows the steps)

# check your system, then try it
emrac doctor             # read-only health checks, with a fix for each finding
emrac search ripgrep
emrac install ripgrep    # preview, confirm, install
emrac undo               # reverse the last transaction

# remove it again
sudo pacman -Rns emrac

items.name: rlae-research
items.description: Runtime low-rank adaptive environments: reversible, modular learning with externalised, auditable behavioural adaptation.
items.body:
## What it is

This is the code and experiment framework behind the paper *On the Structural Limitations of Weight-Based Neural Adaptation and the Role of Reversible Behavioral Learning*. It is a lightweight runtime environment for dynamic adapter routing and modular parameter isolation, and it is shared strictly so the results can be reproduced.

The idea in one line: learning that cannot be undone is not intelligence, it is a surrender to emergence.

## What it implements

- **Runtime Low-Rank Adaptive Environments (RLAE).** The base model stays permanently frozen, and all adaptive behaviour lives in LoRA modules, so nothing in the base weights is ever changed.
- **Structural Variance Analysis for Robustness (SVAR).** A diagnostic evaluation only: it measures how the system behaves under perturbation and changes nothing.

The experiments use Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct as the base model, with quantized execution supported. One experiment trains and then verifies that a reset restores the original behaviour, and another runs the structural robustness diagnostics.

## Cite and reuse

The paper is on arXiv and the archived version is on Zenodo, both linked above. The repository is a research artifact, so external contributions are not accepted.
items.install:
pip install -r experiments/requirements.txt
python src/exp1_reset/1_baseline.py
python src/exp1_reset/2_train_sft.py
python src/exp1_reset/3_train_rl.py
python src/exp1_reset/4_verify_reset.py     # check the reset really restores the model

items.name: lease-manager-bpctf2
items.description: Self-service cloud provisioning and lease management for CTF challenge infrastructure.
items.body:
## What it was

Lease Manager was a self-service cloud provisioning and lease system built for BPCTF2, a live capture-the-flag event. Instead of organisers handing out infrastructure by hand, players asked for a challenge instance through a web page. The service handled the request, called the infrastructure control tool, and returned the endpoint it had allocated.

It was designed for a live event, where requests arrive at the same time and abuse prevention matters.

## How it worked

- **A small Python service** using only the standard library handled the lease API, with Nginx in front for TLS and reverse proxying. It ran as a systemd service that restarted itself.
- **Two control tools** managed the underlying challenge infrastructure, running on Docker and Docker Compose.
- **Idempotent leases.** Asking again for a team that already had a lease returned the existing one. That also stopped duplicates when a slow cold start, about 10 to 25 seconds, outlasted the client's timeout.
- **Rate limits** in the application: at most 5 distinct team names per address per hour and 12 requests per minute.

## A deliberate trade-off

The deployment did not verify identity at the lease endpoint, because the event was already running and a usable self-service path mattered more. The cost was that someone could, in principle, request a lease under another team's name. It was covered by the rate limits, the existing-lease check, monitoring, and the ability for organisers to quarantine an abused slot.

It ran on Google Cloud Compute Engine, with SSH through Identity-Aware Proxy and Let's Encrypt certificates. The event is over, so the repository is archived.

## The code

The lease service is one Python file I wrote, `leased.py`, using only the standard library. Two parts matter most, shown here as excerpts with the longer messages shortened.

**Abuse control without logins.** The event had already started, so there were no per-team codes. Instead each address may claim only a few distinct team names per hour, and sends only so many requests per minute. Asking again for the same team is free (`leased.py`).

```python
MAX_NEW_TEAMS_PER_IP = 5
WINDOW_SECONDS = 3600
MAX_REQUESTS_PER_IP_PER_MIN = 12

def rate_limit_check(ip: str, team: str) -> str | None:
    """Returns an error string if this request should be rejected, else None."""
    with _lock:
        reqs = _prune(_req_log.get(ip, []), 60)
        if len(reqs) >= MAX_REQUESTS_PER_IP_PER_MIN:
            return "too many requests, slow down"
        reqs.append(time.time())
        _req_log[ip] = reqs

        seen = _known_teams_per_ip.setdefault(ip, set())
        if team not in seen:
            claims = _prune(_new_team_log.get(ip, []), WINDOW_SECONDS)
            if len(claims) >= MAX_NEW_TEAMS_PER_IP:
                return f"too many different team names from this address recently (max {MAX_NEW_TEAMS_PER_IP}/hour)"
            claims.append(time.time())
            _new_team_log[ip] = claims
            seen.add(team)
    return None
```

**Idempotent leases.** A repeat request returns the team's existing lease, and every failure the control tool can report is turned into a clear message and the right status code, so players know what to do next.

```python
def get_or_create_lease(team: str) -> tuple[int, dict]:
    show = run_ctl("show", team)
    if show.returncode == 0:
        info = PARSERS[MODE](show.stdout)
        if info:
            info["status"] = "existing"
            return 200, info

    lease = run_ctl("lease", team)
    out = lease.stdout + lease.stderr
    if lease.returncode != 0:
        if "already had a lease" in out:
            return 409, {"error": "this team already used its lease for this event"}
        if "mid-operation" in out:
            return 503, {"error": "your previous request is still being created, try again in a few seconds"}
        if "pool" in out.lower() and ("full" in out.lower() or "no free" in out.lower()):
            return 503, {"error": "the lease pool is full right now, try again in a few minutes"}
        return 500, {"error": "could not create a lease; an organizer has been notified"}
    ...
```

notes.rate_limit_check: Called before any lease is created. Returns an error message to reject the request, or None to let it through.
notes._lock: One lock around the whole check, so two simultaneous requests from the same address cannot both slip under a limit.
notes._prune: Drops log entries older than the window, so the counters only ever describe the recent past.
notes.MAX_NEW_TEAMS_PER_IP: One address may claim at most this many different team names per window. Stops one machine from hoarding leases under many names.
notes.WINDOW_SECONDS: Length of the sliding window for the new-team limit: one hour.
notes.MAX_REQUESTS_PER_IP_PER_MIN: Plain request rate limit per address, checked over the last 60 seconds.
notes.setdefault: Returns the set of team names this address has used before, creating an empty one the first time.
notes.get_or_create_lease: Idempotent: asking again returns the existing lease instead of making a second one. Returns an HTTP status and a JSON body.
notes.run_ctl: Runs the lease controller command-line tool. All lease state lives there, so this service holds none of it.
notes.PARSERS: Output parsers by deployment mode, so the same endpoint works for each backend.
notes.MODE: Which backend this instance runs against.
notes.if team not in seen: Only a new name for this address counts towards the new-team limit. Reusing a name is free.
notes.len(reqs) >= MAX_REQUESTS_PER_IP_PER_MIN: Too many requests in the last minute: reject before doing any work.
notes.200: OK: a lease already exists, so hand its details back.
notes.409: Conflict: this team already used its one lease for the event, so it is refused rather than given another.
notes.503: Try again later. Either the earlier request is still being created or the pool has no free slot.
notes.500: Anything unexpected. The player sees a generic message and an organizer is notified.
notes.\"already had a lease\": Text the controller prints when a team is repeating itself. Matching it turns that into a clear 409.
notes.\"mid-operation\": The controller is still building this team's lease, so ask the player to wait instead of starting another.

items.name: ndra-pii
items.description: A multi-agent system that finds personal data in documents, scores the risk and redacts it. Built with Kandukoori Tejaswini, on top of NDRA.
items.body:
## What it does

NDRA-PII reads unstructured documents (PDF, DOCX, text and email), finds personally identifiable information, judges how risky each finding is, and writes a redacted copy. It is not a regex filter: a chain of small agents each does one job.

- **Ingestion** reads the file.
- **Classifier** finds PII using Presidio, spaCy and regular expressions together.
- **Fusion** merges overlapping findings, for example "New York" and "New York City".
- **Policy** applies configurable rules, written in YAML, to give each finding a risk score and an action.
- **Redaction** carries the actions out and produces the sanitised document.

Every decision leaves an audit trail, and a frozen mode accepts only the ingestion paths that have been verified end to end, quarantining everything else.

## Where it comes from

It grew out of [NDRA](/projects/ndra), the document research assistant we built earlier. The repository lives under Kandukoori Tejaswini's account and carries that whole history.

## What I did

I wrote 268 of the commits, from August 2025 to July 2026.

- **Deployment, from the start.** The first work was getting the pipeline running for real: the process file, the requirements and the Chroma vector store hosted on Railway.
- **The email parser.** In March 2026 I implemented an RFC-compliant email parser that handles MIME boundaries safely and decodes encodings properly, then merged it in.
- **Cleanup and reproducibility.** I restructured the code for readability and set up a Nix flake for a reproducible environment.
- **The stable release.** I cut the v1.0 stable release on 30 March 2026.
- **The paper.** I worked on the accompanying paper in April 2026.

## Who else

Kandukoori Tejaswini, who owns the repository, made around 24 commits, including the Docker setup with health checks. Karedla Rupa Yeshvitha made 4. The project is licensed GPL-3.0.

## The Code

These are excerpts, shortened. The email parser is the file I wrote, `core/v2/parsers/rfc_email_parser.py`. It exists because redacting an email as plain text corrupted the message structure in 29% of cases in a review of the earlier approach: a pattern could match a MIME boundary or a header and break the email. The parser reads the message properly, collects everything that must not be touched, and rebuilds the email after redaction.

**Finding what must never be redacted** (`rfc_email_parser.py`).

```python
def _extract_mime_boundaries(self, msg: Message) -> List[str]:
    """MIME boundaries define message structure and MUST NOT be redacted."""
    boundaries = []
    if msg.is_multipart():
        boundary = msg.get_boundary()
        if boundary:
            boundaries.append(boundary)
        for part in msg.walk():
            if part.is_multipart():
                boundary = part.get_boundary()
                if boundary:
                    boundaries.append(boundary)
    return boundaries

def get_protected_strings(self, parsed: ParsedEmail) -> List[str]:
    protected = []
    for boundary in parsed.mime_boundaries:
        protected.append(boundary)
        protected.append(f"--{boundary}")
        protected.append(f"--{boundary}--")
    protected.extend(["Content-Type:", "Content-Transfer-Encoding:", "MIME-Version:"])
    return protected
```

**Putting the email back together.** Only the readable body is replaced. Attachments and structure are left alone, and the original encoding is reapplied (`rfc_email_parser.py`).

```python
def reconstruct(self, parsed: ParsedEmail, redacted_text: str) -> bytes:
    msg = parsed.raw_message
    if msg.is_multipart():
        for part in msg.walk():
            content_type = part.get_content_type()
            content_disposition = str(part.get("Content-Disposition", ""))
            if "attachment" in content_disposition:
                continue
            if content_type == "text/plain":
                self._set_part_payload(part, redacted_text, parsed)
                break
    else:
        if msg.get_content_type() == "text/plain":
            self._set_part_payload(msg, redacted_text, parsed)
    return msg.as_bytes(policy=self.policy)
```

If strict parsing fails, a best-effort fallback still returns the text, with the error recorded in a header, so one bad email never stops a batch.

notes._extract_mime_boundaries: Collects every MIME boundary string in the message, including the ones in nested parts.
notes.get_protected_strings: Builds the list of strings the redactor must never touch.
notes.reconstruct: Puts the redacted text back into the original message, so the output is still a valid email.
notes.is_multipart: True when the message has several parts, such as plain text, HTML and attachments.
notes.get_boundary: The delimiter string between the parts of a multipart message.
notes.walk: Visits the message and every nested part in order.
notes.ParsedEmail: The parsed form of the message: its parts, headers and boundaries.
notes._set_part_payload: Writes the redacted text into one part, keeping that part's encoding and charset.
notes.as_bytes: Serialises the message back to bytes using the original policy, so line endings and headers stay as they were.
notes.\"\"\"MIME boundaries define message str: If a boundary were redacted as if it were personal data, the email would no longer parse. This is the reason for the whole function.
notes.f\"--{boundary}--\": The closing delimiter of a multipart message. The opening one is the same without the trailing dashes.
notes.\"attachment\": Attachments are skipped here. The redactor only rewrites the readable text body.
notes.\"text/plain\": Only the plain-text part is rewritten. Other parts are left exactly as they came.
notes.\"Content-Transfer-Encoding:\": Header names are protected too, so a name like this is never mistaken for personal data.

items.name: ndra
items.description: Neuro-Semantic Document Research Assistance: asks a long document a vague question and answers with the clause that decides it. Archived; it became NDRA-PII.
items.body:
## What it was

NDRA took a vague question about a long policy document, for example "46-year-old male, knee surgery in Pune, 3-month-old policy", pulled out the structured facts, found the clauses that apply, and returned a decision as JSON: approved or rejected, the amount, and the clause that justifies it.

## How it worked

A four-stage pipeline: preprocessing and chunking, embeddings stored in a Chroma vector database, query understanding and intent mapping, and a retrieval-augmented generation step with decision logic. Chunking respected meaning rather than size, and every answer traced back to the source chunks. The target was an answer in under 8 seconds, reached with parallel processing, a fast model through OpenRouter and a Gemini fallback.

## What I did

I wrote 115 of the commits, in July and August 2025. My work was the language side and the deployment:

- understanding the natural-language query and restructuring it,
- mapping the structured query to intent and fields,
- the retrieval and answer pipeline,
- fixing the dependency conflicts between the libraries,
- deploying it, with Chroma hosted on Railway.

It was built by a team, as Team NDRA. Kandukoori Tejaswini made two commits. The repository is archived, and the work continues in [NDRA-PII](/projects/ndra-pii).

## The Code

Excerpts, trimmed for length (debug output removed, and the Gemini branch simplified).

**Turning a question into fields.** After the language model extracts what it can, plain code decides what the user is asking for, structures it, and scores how complete the question was, so the pipeline knows when to ask for more (`strqgen.py`).

```python
def classify_intent(query: str) -> str:
    intent_keywords = {
        "eligibility_check": ["eligible", "eligibility", "can i", "still covered"],
        "claim_status": ["claim status", "track claim", "claim update"],
        "coverage_check": ["covered", "coverage", "what is included"],
        "renewal": ["renew", "extension", "renewal"],
        "premium_info": ["premium", "cost", "price", "installment"],
        "document_requirement": ["documents", "papers", "required for"],
    }
    query_lower = query.lower()
    for intent, keywords in intent_keywords.items():
        if any(kw in query_lower for kw in keywords):
            return intent
    return "general_inquiry"

def compute_completeness_score(structured_query: dict) -> float:
    fields = ["subject", "age", "gender", "procedure", "location", "policy_duration"]
    filled = sum(1 for field in fields if structured_query.get(field))
    return round(filled / len(fields), 2)
```

**Fast model first, Gemini as the fallback.** Search runs against the Chroma store, the chunks are trimmed in parallel, and if the fast model fails the same prompt goes to Gemini. Only if both fail does the request error (`ragqexec.py`).

```python
def semantic_search_parallel(query: str, top_k=5):
    query_vec = embed_func(query)
    results = collection.query(query_embeddings=[query_vec], n_results=top_k)
    raw_chunks = results["documents"][0]
    metadatas = results["metadatas"][0]

    def clean(c): return " ".join(c.strip().split())[:400]
    with ThreadPoolExecutor() as executor:
        trimmed_chunks = list(executor.map(clean, raw_chunks))
    return trimmed_chunks, metadatas

def generate_llm_response(prompt: str) -> str:
    try:
        return fast_chat(prompt)
    except Exception as fast_error:
        print(f"Fast LLM failed, falling back to Gemini: {fast_error}")
        try:
            model = genai.GenerativeModel("gemini-2.5-flash-lite")
            response = model.generate_content(prompt)
            if hasattr(response, "text") and response.text:
                return response.text.strip()
            raise ValueError(f"Unexpected Gemini response structure: {response}")
        except Exception as gemini_error:
            raise RuntimeError(f"Both LLMs failed. Gemini error: {gemini_error}")
```

**Showing which clause decided it.** Every answer carries the three source clauses closest to its own justification, so the user can check the reasoning (`ragqexec.py`).

```python
def trace_supporting_clauses(justification: str, clauses: list[str], top_k: int = 3):
    scored = [(i, SequenceMatcher(None, justification.lower(), clause.lower()).ratio())
              for i, clause in enumerate(clauses)]
    top_indices = sorted(scored, key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)[:top_k]
    return [clauses[i] for i, _ in top_indices]
```

notes.classify_intent: Rule-based first pass: decides what the user is asking for without calling a model.
notes.intent_keywords: Each intent and the phrases that signal it. Cheap, predictable, and easy to extend.
notes.compute_completeness_score: How much of the query has the details the pipeline needs, as a fraction from 0 to 1.
notes.semantic_search_parallel: Embeds the question and fetches the closest policy chunks from the vector store.
notes.collection.query: Vector similarity search over the embedded policy documents.
notes.ThreadPoolExecutor: Cleans the retrieved chunks on several threads at once.
notes.executor.map: Applies clean to every chunk in parallel and keeps the original order.
notes.generate_llm_response: Tries the fast model first. If it fails, falls back to Gemini, and raises only if both fail.
notes.trace_supporting_clauses: Finds which policy clauses back up the model's justification, by text similarity.
notes.SequenceMatcher: Standard-library fuzzy matcher. Gives a similarity ratio between two strings.
notes.top_k: How many results to keep: the closest few, not everything.
notes.round(filled / len(fields), 2): Share of the six fields that are filled in, to two decimals.
notes.\"gemini-2.5-flash-lite\": Light, cheap Gemini model used only as the fallback.
notes.[:400]: Cut each chunk to 400 characters, so the prompt stays small.
notes.return \"general_inquiry\": Nothing matched, so it is treated as a general question.

items.name: phishvault
items.description: A platform for investigating, managing and analysing suspicious links. A collaboration with Kandukoori Tejaswini; I built the backend.
items.body:
## What it is

PhishVault helps someone investigate, manage and analyse potentially malicious URLs, with static and dynamic analysis behind a web interface. The stack is Go, React and TypeScript, MongoDB, Docker and Puppeteer. It is a collaboration and the repository lives under Kandukoori Tejaswini's account. Version 2 is still in development.

## What I did

I wrote 155 of the commits to Tejaswini's 43, and the backend was my side of it from the first day, 28 May 2025.

- **The backend, and the first version.** Backend work from the first day, then error handling, the report on a test site, and a recorded demonstration.
- **Version 2, in February 2026.** The scan report page with its backend API, a screenshot viewer, and a graph visualiser for the results.
- **Reliability.** I fixed the race conditions that happened at start-up.
- **Documentation.** I wrote the Phase 2 implementation report covering the infrastructure, backend and command line.

## What Tejaswini built

The frontend, the ingestion service with its API for submitting URLs, emails and files, user authentication, and the scan management screens, plus a document on improving the risk scoring.

## The Code

Excerpts from files I wrote or mostly wrote, shortened.

**Grouping scans into campaigns.** Phishing kits are cloned, so scans of the same campaign look alike. I wrote the clustering that groups them with DBSCAN, using a distance that mixes three signals: the visual hash of the page (weighted most, since a cloned page looks the same), whether the servers share a subnet, and how many page-structure tokens overlap (`services/analysis/clustering/dbscan.go`).

```go
// distance calculates the "Campaign Similarity" (0.0 = Identical, 1.0 = Different).
func distance(a, b *FeatureVector) float64 {
	// 1. Visual distance: Hamming distance on the 64-bit perceptual hash, scaled to 0..1
	visualDist := float64(hamming(a.VisualHash, b.VisualHash)) / 64.0

	// 2. Infrastructure: 0.0 if the same /24 subnet, 1.0 otherwise
	ipDist := 1.0
	if isSameSubnet(a.IP, b.IP) {
		ipDist = 0.0
	}

	// 3. Page structure: Jaccard distance over the key DOM tokens
	domDist := jaccardDistance(a.DOMTokens, b.DOMTokens)

	// Visual is the strongest indicator of a phishing kit (cloned UI).
	// Weight: Visual 60%, IP 20%, DOM 20%
	return (visualDist * 0.6) + (ipDist * 0.2) + (domDist * 0.2)
}
```

**One path for every artifact.** The orchestrator takes anything submitted, analyses it by type, asks a policy engine for the verdict, adds the result to the campaign graph, and buffers it for clustering. If the graph database is down it falls back to a console adapter instead of failing (`services/analysis/orchestrator.go`).

```go
switch input.ArtifactType {
case "URL":
	similarity, urgency, intent, hasLoginForm, domainAgeDays, visualHash = o.analyzeURL(ctx, &input)
case "EMAIL":
	sig := AnalyzeEmail(input)
	input.Signals = append(input.Signals, sig)
	urgency, intent = sig.Weight, "EmailPotentialPhish"
case "FILE":
	sig := AnalyzeFile(input)
	input.Signals = append(input.Signals, sig)
	urgency, intent = sig.Weight, "FilePotentialPhish"
}

verdict, err := decision.EvaluateVerdict(ctx, decision.PolicyInput{
	VisualMatchScore: similarity,
	UrgencyScore:     urgency,
	Intent:           intent,
	HasLoginForm:     hasLoginForm,
	DomainAgeDays:    domainAgeDays,
})
input.Verdict, input.RiskScore = verdict.Verdict, verdict.RiskScore

o.graphProjector.ProjectSAL(input)   // add it to the campaign graph
o.bufferForClustering(input, visualHash)
```

Scoring and verdicts come from an OPA policy engine, so the rules can change without recompiling the service.

notes.distance: How far apart two submissions are as campaigns. 0 means the same kit, 1 means unrelated.
notes.hamming: Counts the bits that differ between two 64-bit perceptual hashes. Similar-looking pages differ in few bits.
notes.isSameSubnet: True when both addresses sit in the same /24, a sign they were hosted together.
notes.jaccardDistance: 1 minus the overlap of two token sets. Pages built from the same kit share most of their tokens.
notes.FeatureVector: The few numbers each page is reduced to: visual hash, hosting address and DOM tokens.
notes.AnalyzeEmail: Scores an email on its own signals. No page is fetched.
notes.AnalyzeFile: Scores an uploaded file on its own signals.
notes.EvaluateVerdict: Hands the signals to the policy engine, which decides the verdict and the risk score.
notes.PolicyInput: All the evidence the policy sees, in one struct.
notes.ProjectSAL: Adds the submission to the campaign graph, so later lookalikes connect to it.
notes.bufferForClustering: Queues the submission for the batch job that groups similar pages into campaigns.
notes.analyzeURL: Fetches and inspects the page: visual hash, login form, domain age.
notes.switch: Different artifact types take different analysis paths but end in the same verdict call.
notes./ 64.0: Hash is 64 bits, so dividing scales the distance to 0..1.
notes.* 0.6: Visual similarity gets 60% of the weight.
notes.* 0.2: Hosting and page structure get 20% each.
notes.1.0: Default is the maximum distance: a different network, unless the check below proves otherwise.
notes.0.0: Same subnet: no distance on this signal.

items.name: project-ouroboros
items.description: A modular ESP32 platform for wireless defence and monitoring, with a 15-day expo prototype. Archived.

notes.startAsyncScan: Kicks off a Wi-Fi scan without blocking the main loop. Retries on a driver state conflict, and escalates to a full driver rebuild after three failed attempts in a row.
notes.wifi_scan_config_t: ESP-IDF struct that holds the scan settings: hidden networks, active vs passive, dwell time per channel.
notes.WIFI_SCAN_TYPE_ACTIVE: Active scan: the board sends probe requests and waits for answers, which is faster and finds more than listening passively.
notes.esp_wifi_scan_start: Starts the scan. The second argument false means non-blocking: it returns at once and the driver raises a scan-done event later.
notes.ESP_ERR_WIFI_STATE: The driver is in a state that does not allow the call, for example a scan is already running. Usually fixed by restarting the driver.
notes.esp_wifi_stop: Stops the Wi-Fi driver without freeing it. The light fix for a stuck state.
notes.esp_wifi_start: Starts the driver again after a stop.
notes.vTaskDelay: FreeRTOS delay that yields the CPU to other tasks while it waits, unlike a busy-wait delay().
notes.pdMS_TO_TICKS: Converts milliseconds to FreeRTOS ticks, so the delay is right whatever the tick rate is.
notes.scanFailCount: Counts failed scans in a row. Reaching 3 means the light recovery is not working.
notes.fullWifiRecovery: The heavy fix: tear the whole Wi-Fi stack down and bring it back, so the board heals without a reboot.
notes.esp_wifi_deinit: Frees the driver and its buffers completely. After this the driver must be initialised again.
notes.esp_wifi_init: Allocates and initialises the Wi-Fi driver from a config struct.
notes.WIFI_MODE_APSTA: Station and access point at once: the board scans and joins networks while also hosting its own dashboard network.
notes.esp_wifi_set_storage: WIFI_STORAGE_RAM keeps Wi-Fi config in RAM only, so it does not wear the flash on every change.
notes.esp_event_handler_instance_register: Subscribes onScanDone to the driver's scan-done event and returns a handle that can be removed later.
notes.esp_event_handler_instance_unregister: Removes the old subscription first, so recovery never leaves two handlers firing for one event.
notes.scan_done_handler_instance: Handle for the registered scan-done callback, kept so it can be unregistered during recovery.
notes.WS_EVT_CONNECT: A dashboard just connected to the WebSocket.
notes.WS_EVT_DATA: A WebSocket message arrived from the dashboard.
notes.updateClients: Pushes the current access point and station lists to every connected dashboard.
notes.deserializeJson: ArduinoJson parse. Returns an error code, so a failed parse (not JSON) falls through to the raw-command branch.
notes.StaticJsonDocument: JSON document on a fixed 512-byte stack buffer, so parsing a message never touches the heap.
notes.onCommand: Callback into the firmware's own command line. The dashboard and a serial terminal drive the same commands.
notes.serializeJson: Writes the acknowledgement document back out as a string.
notes.AwsFrameInfo: WebSocket frame metadata: opcode, whether the message is complete, its length.
notes.// non-blocking: The call returns immediately. The result arrives later as a scan-done event, so the display and web server never freeze during a scan.
notes.// anything else: log it and stop spinni: Any other error will not be fixed by retrying, so give up on this attempt rather than loop forever.
notes.// persistent failures: rebuild the driv: Three scans in a row failed, so the light restart is not enough. Escalate to the full rebuild.
notes.// state conflict: light recovery, let t: The cheap fix first: bounce the driver, wait for it to settle, then try the scan again.
notes.// send the current state to the new cli: A dashboard that connects mid-scan should see the current lists straight away, not wait for the next scan.
notes.// acknowledge to the dashboard: The dashboard gets an echo of what ran, which it shows in its terminal pane.
notes.maxRetries = 3: Three attempts per scan request. Enough to ride out a transient state clash, low enough not to stall.
notes.150: 150 ms: long enough for the driver to finish stopping before it is started again.
notes.200: 200 ms: settle time after the restart, so the next scan does not hit a half-started driver.
notes.scanFailCount >= 3: Counts only consecutive failures. One success resets it, so rare hiccups never trigger a rebuild.
notes.scan_time.active.max = 300: Wait at most 300 ms per channel for replies. Longer finds slower networks but makes a full sweep take longer.
notes.show_hidden = true: Include networks that do not broadcast their name.
notes.\"OuroMini\": The name of the network the board hosts for the dashboard.
notes.max_connection = 4: At most four devices can be joined to the board's own network at once, which keeps memory use bounded.
notes.info->opcode != WS_TEXT: Only text frames are handled. Binary or control frames are ignored.
notes.strcmp(typeStr, \"exec\") == 0: The message is only treated as a command if its type is exactly "exec".
notes.msg.trim(): Strip stray whitespace and newlines so a pasted command still matches.

items.description: A phishing-simulation event I coordinated and built the environment for, at Malla Reddy University. Archived.

notes.MailHog: Local test mail server. It catches every message, so nothing here can leave the machine.
notes.sleep 2: Gives MailHog a moment to start before the app tries to use it.
notes.&: Runs in the background, so the script can carry on and start the app.
notes.2>&1: Sends errors to the same log file as normal output.
notes.EmailMessage: Standard-library email object: headers and body in one place.
notes.1025: MailHog's SMTP port. A real mail server would never be on this port, so the mail is caught locally.
notes.# local MailHog only: The point of the design: delivery goes to localhost and nowhere else.
notes.@app.route: Binds a URL to a function. Each level of the game is a route.
notes.render_template: Renders the HTML page for that level.
notes.redirect: A POST moves the player on to the next page, and the last page leads to the flag.
notes.methods=['GET', 'POST']: The page loads on GET, and submitting the form is a POST.
notes.# Level 2: two pages, then the flag: Levels get longer: this one chains two pages before the flag.

items.name: ricebtw
items.description: My Linux setup across Arch and Void: Home Manager on top of Arch, and MangoWC with DankMaterialShell on both.
items.body:
## What it is

My whole Linux setup in one repository, across two machines: an Arch Linux daily driver and a Void Linux install I experiment on. It started as `archbtw` and was renamed `ricebtw` on 21 October 2026.

## The two machines

- **Arch Linux** is the daily driver. Arch and pacman still own the kernel, bootloader, drivers, systemd, networking and PipeWire. Nix and Home Manager own the user environment on top: command-line tools, dev toolchains, shell config and dotfiles. It is Home Manager on Arch, not NixOS.
- **Void Linux** is the experiment. It runs runit and xbps, with no systemd, no Nix and no Home Manager. Everything for it is self-contained in `rice/void-linux/`.

Both run MangoWC with DankMaterialShell. Hyprland was replaced by MangoWC in August 2026, and its configs are kept only as legacy reference.

## What is in it

- A Nix flake that pins nixpkgs-unstable, Home Manager and agenix, with the config split into modules: CLI tools, git, zsh, aliases, dev toolchains, secrets, Neovim and GUI apps.
- Plain backup copies of the desktop dotfiles for both distros: MangoWC and DankMaterialShell settings, keybinds, kitty, rofi and notification config, plus the xbps package lists for Void.
- The full wallpaper pool, about 3.7 GB, committed to GitHub and kept out of the local working tree with a sparse checkout so it does not sit on disk twice.

## Where it stands

The Home Manager work is done through the repo skeleton, CLI tools, git, shell, dev toolchains and Neovim, with GUI apps partly done. Fonts, themes and icons were looked at and deliberately left alone, because colour theming is driven by matugen templates.

## Upstream

Moving from Hyprland to MangoWC in August 2026 meant fixing the shell I use. My fix to the MangoWC port of the Caelestia shell was merged upstream: [caelestia-shell-mango](/projects/caelestia-shell-mango).

## The Code for it

The parts that are actual code, not config. Excerpts, with personal paths blacked out with █ and the rest of each file left out.

**One theme change, everything follows.** When the wallpaper changes, the desktop theme changes, and a hook rebuilds my terminal logo in the new colours and redraws it. The hook is two lines (`fastfetch/theme-hook.sh`).

```bash
# theme postHook: rebuild the themed logo, then redraw the focused kitty window (if it is at a bare shell).
# Runs in the background, so it never blocks a wallpaper change.
dir="$(dirname "$(readlink -f "$0")")"
"$dir/make-ultron-logo.sh" && "$dir/redraw-focused-kitty.py"
```

**Redrawing only where it is safe.** The redraw script types `clear && fastfetch` into a terminal, which would wreck anything running there. So it only touches a window that is focused and whose only foreground processes are a bare shell, and does nothing otherwise (`fastfetch/redraw-focused-kitty.py`).

```python
SHELLS = {"zsh", "fish", "bash", "sh", "dash"}
CMD = "clear && fastfetch\r"

for sock in sorted(glob.glob("/tmp/kitty-socket-*")):
    try:
        oses = json.loads(kitty(sock, "ls"))
    except Exception:
        continue  # stale socket or kitty not answering
    for o in oses:
        if not o.get("is_focused"):
            continue
        for tab in o["tabs"]:
            for w in tab["windows"]:
                if not w.get("is_focused"):
                    continue
                fg = [os.path.basename((p.get("cmdline") or ["?"])[0]).lstrip("-")
                      for p in w.get("foreground_processes", [])]
                if not fg or any(f not in SHELLS for f in fg):
                    print(f"skip window {w['id']}: foreground = {fg}")
                    continue
                kitty(sock, "send-text", "--match", f"id:{w['id']}", CMD)
```

**Colours from whatever theme is active.** The logo script picks its accent from the theme's primary colour, trying three sources in order and falling back to red if none exist. It then shifts the hue of the red logo to match and uses brightness as transparency, so the black background disappears (`fastfetch/make-ultron-logo.sh`).

```python
def load():
    # 1. DMS/matugen template output
    try:
        d = json.load(open(os.path.expanduser("~/.cache/matugen/fastfetch-colors.json")))
        return {"primary": d["primary"], "onSurface": d["on_surface"]}
    except Exception:
        pass
    # 2. legacy caelestia hook / scheme file
    try:
        return json.loads(os.environ["SCHEME_COLOURS"])
    except Exception:
        pass
    try:
        return json.load(open(os.path.expanduser("~/.local/state/caelestia/scheme.json")))["colours"]
    except Exception:
        return {}

h, l, s = colorsys.rgb_to_hls(*rgb(cols["primary"]))
accent = hexc(*colorsys.hls_to_rgb(h, 0.62, max(s, 0.7)))
dim    = hexc(*colorsys.hls_to_rgb(h, 0.42, max(s, 0.55)))
```

```bash
# hue-shift the red to the accent hue; brightness -> alpha so the black background disappears
magick "$SRC" -alpha off -modulate 100,100,"$HUEARG" \
    \( "$SRC" -alpha off -colorspace Gray -level 4%,45% \) \
    -compose CopyOpacity -composite "$TMP/logo.png"
```

**Tap Super to open the launcher.** A small script that does this without grabbing the keyboard, so combos like Super+D still reach the compositor. A tap is a press and release under 0.35 seconds with nothing else pressed in between (`bin/super-tap`). It is started at login from `/home/████████/.local/bin/super-tap`.

```python
TAP_MAX = 0.35

def handle(code, value):
    global meta_down
    if value == 2:  # autorepeat
        return
    if code in (KEY_LEFTMETA, KEY_RIGHTMETA):
        if value == 1:
            meta_down = time.monotonic()
        elif value == 0 and meta_down is not None:
            if time.monotonic() - meta_down <= TAP_MAX:
                subprocess.Popen(cmd, stdout=subprocess.DEVNULL, stderr=subprocess.DEVNULL)
            meta_down = None
    elif value == 1:  # any other key / mouse button / touch while Super held
        meta_down = None
```

**Cursor follows focus across monitors.** Moving focus to the next monitor also puts the pointer in the middle of it, using the monitor's position, size and scale (`hypr/scripts/focus_next_monitor.sh`, from the Hyprland days).

```bash
monitor=$(hyprctl monitors -j | jq '.[] | select(.focused == true)')
x=$(echo "$monitor" | jq '.x + (.width / 2 / .scale)' | bc)
y=$(echo "$monitor" | jq '.y + (.height / 2 / .scale)' | bc)
```

notes.readlink -f: Resolves symlinks, so the script finds its siblings wherever the theme tool runs it from.
notes.# Runs in the background, so it never bl: The hook is slow work. It runs detached so changing the wallpaper stays instant.
notes.SHELLS: Foreground programs that count as a bare prompt. Anything else is left alone.
notes.CMD: What gets typed into the window: clear the screen, then run fastfetch.
notes.glob.glob: Finds every running kitty instance through its control socket.
notes.is_focused: Only the window you are looking at is touched.
notes.foreground_processes: What is running in the window right now. If it is not a shell, something like an editor is open, so the redraw is skipped.
notes.send-text: Types the command into that window as if the user had.
notes.# stale socket or kitty not answering: A leftover socket from a closed kitty is not an error. Skip it.
notes.rgb_to_hls: Converts the colour to hue, lightness, saturation, so lightness can be set without changing the hue.
notes.max(s, 0.7): Never let the accent go washed out: at least 70% saturation.
notes.0.42: Lightness for the dimmer shade of the same hue.
notes.-modulate 100,100,\"$HUEARG\": Keeps brightness and saturation, rotates only the hue, to the theme colour.
notes.-level 4%,45%: Stretches the dark-to-mid range of the grey copy, which becomes the transparency.
notes.-compose CopyOpacity: Uses the grey copy as the alpha channel: dark pixels turn transparent, so the black background disappears.
notes.TAP_MAX: A press shorter than this counts as a tap. Longer is a hold.
notes.0.35: Seconds. About as long as a quick tap takes.
notes.time.monotonic: Clock that never jumps when the system time changes, so the timing is reliable.
notes.meta_down: When Super went down, or None. Any other input while it is held cancels the tap.
notes.jq: Picks the focused monitor out of the JSON.
notes.# 1. DMS/matugen template output: First choice: colours generated from the wallpaper.
notes.# 2. legacy caelestia hook / scheme file: Fallbacks, so the script still works on older setups.
notes.# autorepeat: A held key sends repeats. They are not presses.
notes.# any other key / mouse button / touch w: Super was used as a modifier, not tapped alone, so the launcher must not open.

items.name: caelestia-shell-mango
items.description: The Caelestia desktop shell on MangoWC. My merged fix made every drawer toggle work again.

notes.TypeError: The shell code was written for Hyprland and assumed values only Hyprland provides. Under Mango they came back null.
notes.monitorFor: Looks up the monitor for a screen. Other code uses the result as a key.
notes.focusedMonitor: The one monitor object, created once, so every read gets the same instance.
notes.QtObject: A persistent QML object. Unlike a property literal, it keeps one identity.
notes.readonly: Callers can read these properties but not overwrite them.
notes.monitors.values.map: Hyprland's monitor list is a model with a values array. Mango's is a plain array, so .values is not a function.
notes.monitors.map(e => e.name): The fix: map the array directly.
notes.return root.focusedMonitor;: Same object every call. Returning a fresh literal each time would never match the key in the Map.
notes.Visibilities.qml: Stores per-monitor state in a Map keyed by the monitor object itself, so the object's identity matters.
notes.// single-monitor-only, so return the sa: The Mango backend only handles one monitor, so one shared object is enough.
